Talullas: The only plate in the sweep with no starch on it at all: char-grilled salmon on arugula, with haydari doing the job cacık does at Bosphorus. Refusing the bread is the whole edit. The gap is fibre — this is fish, leaves and yogurt.
Alpaca Peruvian Charcoal Chicken: Two sides are included, and black beans and house salad sit in the same tier as fries and white rice. Take them and a quarter bird is 53 g of protein for $11.29. The ají verde is mayonnaise; refusing it costs about a point of flavour.
Carmen's Cuban Cafe & Lounge: Every entrée here arrives with three sides, and that is what sinks the braises — rice, beans and maduros add 400 calories before the meat does anything. Moving the ceviche onto the house salad skips all of it. Quiet, clean, faintly under-seasoned.
Flame Kabob: The menu itself offers salad in place of the chelo, so the best move is a printed option rather than a negotiation. One breast skewer is 46 g of protein, and the $7.99 cucumber yogurt is a live-culture bowl rather than a ramekin. Breast is the driest skewer they grill.
Pupuseria Doña Laura: Curtido comes with every pupusa order — and only with pupusas, which is the finding. Order the grilled breast and you lose the ferment entirely. Whether they will sell curtido apart from a pupusa order could not be established, so it is scored here as though they will not.
Twisted Noodles: Grilled, dressed rather than sauced, and sent without rice, so 35 g of protein arrives at 370 calories. Nothing is stripped, so everything lands. The fish sauce is what keeps it off the podium at 1,960 mg.
Mum's Jamaican Restaurant: Ordered steamed rather than brown-stewed, this beats all three existing Caribbean entries by a wide margin: a whole snapper in thyme-and-pimento broth, 63 g of protein under 550 calories. The butter in the broth is the only meaningful fat.
Golden Dragon: Every American Chinese takeout prints a diet menu and nobody orders from it. This one carries its own instruction — steamed, sauce on the side, no oil — which is the entire nutritional argument in eight words. Flavour 1.1 is the honest price.
Kipos Greek Taverna: The archetype arrives assembled: grilled whole-muscle chicken, a live-yogurt tzatziki that is part of the dish rather than an upcharge, and a tomato-cucumber salad. Only the pita is refused. The lemon potatoes hold the score down — whole potato, but a lot of it in a lot of oil.
The Halal Guys: Chicken over salad instead of rice is orderable and nobody orders it. That single swap is the entire entry: 54 g of protein at 400 calories. The white sauce is the other half of the decision and it is declined here.
Road To Myanmar Asian Cuisine: Laphet is genuinely fermented tea leaf, which is why this scores 6.8 on gut — the highest of anything added in this edition. It is also 1,680 mg of sodium, because the same fermentation that earns the gut score is a salt-preservation method.
Sam Jones BBQ: Sliced turkey breast is the least-ordered thing on a whole-hog board and by a distance the leanest: 55 g of protein for 462 calories. The sweet potato muffin is where a plate like this usually goes wrong, so it is declined. Sodium stays the unfixable part.
Lawrence Barbecue: Smoked then fried, so the wings are not a lean order — but the AP dry rub is the only sugar-light option on a sauce board where everything else is honey, caramel or a wet glaze. Choosing the rub is the whole decision.
Boteco do Brazil: Picanha on the house salad rather than the churrasco plate, which is the difference between one protein and a buffet. The vinaigrette is counted at half, as the build instructs; taken in full it adds 65 calories and 350 mg.
Hady's Restaurant International Cuisine: Suya is dry-rubbed and grilled rather than stewed in palm oil, which is what separates it from everything else on this menu. Collard greens instead of the fries, jollof or fufu is the edit, and it is worth about 400 calories.
Chop Naija Kitchen: The swallow is the calorie problem, not the soup: refuse the pounded yam, fufu and eba entirely and the vegetable soup is 51 g of protein and real leafy-vegetable content. Palm oil keeps saturated fat high whatever you do.
Al's Burger Shack: A grilled chicken sandwich at $10.45 is the cheapest thing added this edition and it scores 4.8, which is roughly what the format allows. Printed because a category that scores badly is information, not because this is a good order.
The Pit Authentic Barbecue: Whole hogs go on the pit overnight, so the chop carries its own fat — that is where 12 g of saturated fat comes from. Cabbage collards and green beans instead of hush puppies and mac, dressed with vinegar-pepper rather than a sweet sauce, holds sugar to 7 g.
Zweli's Ekhaya: Berbere half chicken with the hot honey on the side, which is the one decision that matters — used in full it is the dish's whole sugar figure. Slaw as it comes; no dombolo, no magwinya.
Another Broken Egg Cafe: The only entry added this edition whose figures come from a published nutrition document rather than construction. 630 mg of sodium is the lowest in the group, and 31 g of protein at 550 calories is what an omelette gives you.
Grand Malabar Indian Cuisine: Kappa and meen curry is fish rather than a cream curry, but coconut oil and grated coconut carry 17 g of saturated fat regardless, which is what holds it at 4.8. No priced menu is published anywhere reachable, so the price is approximate.
Dim Sum House: Congee is the lean order on a dim sum menu and almost nobody treats it as the main event. Fish rather than pork, gai lan with the oyster sauce halved, and the fried items left alone. Sodium is the ceiling here at 1,780 mg.
The Fiction Kitchen: Seitan carries 42 g of protein, which is the argument for a vegan kitchen appearing in a protein-weighted ranking at all. The bun and the dressed slaw are what hold it at 4.6, and 1,780 mg of sodium is the seitan itself, not a seasoning choice.
Let's Eat Soul Food: Baked rather than fried is a real menu option here and it is the only reason this clears 4.7. Collards and cabbage instead of the cornbread and the mac. At 2,120 mg it is the saltiest thing added this edition.
BLR Food Street: Chaat is assembled from fried components and salted at five separate points — the tikki, the masala, both chutneys, the sev and the dahi. At $10 it is the cheapest dish in the book and it scores 4.0, which is the category's honest ceiling.
Makus Empanadas: Two baked empanadas with beans and a spinach salad rather than a plate of six. Baked rather than fried is the whole edit and it is not enough: pastry is pastry, and 905 calories for 31 g of protein is what that costs.
Pizzeria Toro: A margherita is the leanest thing on a Neapolitan board and it still scores 2.6 — the dough alone carries about 1,475 mg of sodium at the standard 2.5% salt. Printed because the category needed testing, and it failed.
